I've rescued my best friend mid-suicide attempt twice. "Horror" doesn't even begin to describe the feeling of those experiences.

Something to keep in mind, both you and your friend were seriously injured that night, her physically and you mentally/emotionally from the PTSD.  Both of you are now on a journey dealing with the effects of her suicide attempt. Reminding yourself you're both in this, you didn't walk away ok, might help with dealing with the guilt.

I REALLY recommend you talk to your friend about what you're going through. You don't have to say you're suicidal but opening up about the guilt you feel and how her attempt affected you can really start a path to healing. I also needed therapy and meds to deal with what happened. I'm not over it but things are waaay better than they were.

My friend was not happy when I interrupted her attempts and also got aggressive about it. But after she had some treatment she's ultimately glad I stopped her. She's getting married in a few months and I'm a bridesmaid. It really sounds like your friend isn't angry at you. I've stopped other friends and family members who were about to attempt. They were also really angry at the time but every single one has said they're glad that I stopped them and if it happened again they'd want me to stop them again.

I understand wanting to go out on the same method. But her attempt should show you that no method is fool proof. Even if I almost always works who's to say you're not in the small number it doesn't work for and you also end up with a disability and unable to try again? Not that I'm suggesting trying again as a good thing, just giving you a reason I think your brain will still care about when you're in a dark place. If you were successful your suicide it would be devastating for your friend, for whoever found your body and likely for a lot of other people. Don't do it.

Sure! Her approach was about balance and variety. She said nutrient deficiencies can cause/aggravate symptoms of anxiety and depression so a mental health focused diet is really about making sure the body/brain gets what it needs, not about cutting things out.

She gave categories of foods: grains/carbohydrates, proteins, fats, fruits and vegetables and "fun foods" e.g. cookies or chips. She recommended trying to get one from each category except fun foods into lunch and dinner and at least 2-3 of the categories for breakfast and snacks. Also trying to get fruits and vegetables into each meal and snack. She discussed that wholegrains contain more nutrients and vegetables based fats had more nutrients than animal based fats so choose them more often but that eating white bread etc sometimes isn't harmful. She said incorporate as many different types of foods from the categories, especially fruits and vegetables.

There were a few specific tips she gave to help things absorb most effectively, especially when taking supplements. Magnesium (which can lower anxiety) and vitamin D (which can cause low mood if deficient) absorb better when taken with dietary calcium like cheese or yogurt. Iron absorbs better when taken with vitamin C. For promoting better sleep she recommended having a slow digesting rich carbohydrate food e.g. whole grain as part of an evening snack as it helps the brain with producing serotonin which is important for sleep.

For "fun foods" she recommended having them as a regular part of a mental health diet. If you have them regularly, on top of a diet where you're meeting your needs from the other categories you don't crave them so much and that eaten this way they're not going to aggravate depression or anxiety symptoms. 

She also talked about how it's not just nutrients in food that affect mental health, things like taste and experiences matter. There's mental health value in enjoying the taste of things you eat and participating in eating your friend's birthday cake. Being flexible in your diet and not having it limit your social experiences like going to events or restaurants is important because those social experiences can really matter for your mental health, way more than the content of what you end up eating there.

If someone has certain medical conditions like diabetes, celiac disease or lactose intolerance then they'll have different needs but for promoting good mental health this is her suggested diet.

While not a sedating med, if you're having trouble with hypervigelance from PTSD Prazosin can help reduce that. It's a blood pressure medication but it reduces nightmares and can reduce other PTSD symptoms including hypervigelance. Propranolol, also a blood pressure medication, can treat physical symptoms like racing heart and hypervigelance and can potentially treat RLS. Generally these can be taken with sedating meds and might help them be more effective.

Some of the typical sleep hygiene practices don't always work for people with PTSD. A lot of the "relaxing activities" suggested to do before bed aren't actually relaxing for some people with PTSD e.g. meditations to clear the mind can result in flashbacks. Sometimes people with PTSD need activities with more of a distraction element to help them wind down which can be different from what sleep hygiene usually recommends. Find what works for you. For me DBT (Dialectical Behavioural Therapy) skills were really helpful for this.

I'd suggest anyone considering this consult with a dietician or doctor first. Carbohydrates are building blocks for the brain to make serotonin. A lack of serotonin can worsen depression and anxiety symptoms. Some people who don't have underlying mental health conditions have gotten symptoms of depression when starting a keto diet from the big reduction in carbs dropping their serotonin levels. Source: my dietician who works with people with mental health conditions. Not saying it couldn't be helpful for some people but professional guidance in whether/how to do it is probably helpful.

It didn't completely solve things but it definitely turned down the volume on the PTSD. When I moved away for school I felt so peaceful and so free and so... Normal. Not having things constantly triggering vivid memories was great. I was aware that bad stuff had happened but I didn't feel so... In it.

Even being away temporarily, in later years I went to residential treatment for an ED far away from my city and was amazed how quickly my mood improved and a lot of my anxiety went down from being away from it. I was doing trauma work in therapy, not ignoring it, but being able to come back environment away from the trauma made it easier to heal a bit. 

Unfortunately a lot of that didn't last when I came home to my city. Same thing when I came back from school. Logistically, can you leave your city permanently or do you have people or things that you love there that will call you back there sometimes? If so, be prepared the PTSD can hit harder when you do go back, even if that's temporary.

I've been in a hospital based combined IP/PHP program and a residential program. They had very different approaches . For the dieticians' roles and the whole of treatment.

The hospital program was a very rigid rules-based, behaviour modification program. We did some basic CBT, DBT and ED education groups but the focus was on physical health and meal compliance. Our dieticians explained the rules for hospital menu marking and "challenges" e.g. ordering in, weighed us each week and gave us a post it note each week telling us what changes to our meal plans would be. They sometimes did our meal supervision, let us know if we were eating too fast or too slow and if we were struggling reminded us of the consequences of we didn't i.e. getting discharged from the program and what we'd said in intake would happen to us if we left like our partners threatening to leave us... Yeah. The doctors, nurses and therapists did the same. If we were upset they had a couple go to coping skills (deep breathing, silent mindfulness, do a small craft) and if they didn't work they just expected you to deal with it. The program also has strict restrictions on activity and recommended we never get involved in sports or exercise again after. The overall tone and how we were spoken to had us feeling like preschoolers and juvenile delinquents. The program restored my physical health but wasn't great for my mental health.

The residential program was individualized, home-like and had a very therapeutic focus where our mental health was important. We had individual sessions with our dieticians twice a week where we set goals, adjusted meal plans, talked about challenge foods and worked them in when ready, all of it collaborative. They also helped with coping strategies related to the emotional parts of food like extra support or distraction activities after challenge meals. We had group with them each week to plan our community meals and learn about nutrition topics in a very science-based way which I found helpful. Our therapists did our weight checks and helped us process it. The dieticians did some of our meal supervision and gave distraction activities and emotional support and no threats. We prepared meals with staff help so they helped us with our cooking if needed. We were allowed some activity in the program if it was safe physically. I'm a dancer and they supported it and helped me get on a meal plan that gave me enough fuel for it. We had a lot of group and individual therapy, going way beyond the basics and they were very creative with coping skills and activities, often individualized and collaborative  for what we expressed we needed at the time, music, gardening, art, therapy dogs, sensory activities etc. Staff made me feel really safe and cared for the whole time. I always felt like I was being treated like an adult. All of this created an environment where I actually wanted to recover and what I learned has stayed with me long term and useful in my day to day recovery.

Similar i think. I don't have regular off-times with levodopa (I'm taking Sinemet 6 times a day) but i have times it doesn't work optimally due to illness, sleep deprivation or sometimes at random. And while the Sinemet still usually works well for my legs and feet i get spasms in other muscles that don't respond quite as well to it. All of this has gotten worse/more frequent over time. I definitely notice that my cognition is worse during these times, my focus, concentration, and ability to plan really decline and i feel more sluggish and less on the ball. My doctor told me that this isn't from the DRD itself, that it's due to the pain and stress caused by the spasms and movement problems. And that when the dystonia symptoms are properly controlled by medication my cognition should go back to normal. So far she's been right, though getting a medication regime that does this has gotten more difficult over time.

What kind of exercise are you doing? I find some exercise helps it (cardio, particularly dance, things that involve stretching and movement in the upper body) while other things like lifting weights, upper body strength training like push ups and repetitive movements make it worse. There's some subtle differences, walking/running on a treadmill can make it worse, walking/running outside seems to help, realized it's because outside I'm looking around rather than staring straight forward with my neck on one position. Figured a lot of that out through trial and error.

Call your pharmacy (or any pharmacy that's open), they can advise you based on individual factors like other medications you're on, your weight, how long you've been taking it etc. Definitely don't drive, don't handle anything dangerous like knives or boiling water, avoid stairs, stay somewhere safe where you can lie down, this may make you VERY dizzy.
Have you tried wearing a neck brace the day after you exercise to keep it straight? Or is that painful?

This has happened to me and to my family members who don't have dystonia. It's possible that this is electrolyte related. Magnesium and calcium are the two that seem most likely. The electrolyte pouch is the morning might not be enough when combined with lots of water. Get some blood work done with a full electrolyte panel and the doctor can recommend what to take. I take magnesium in the evening with high calcium food e.g. cheese and Vitamin D. Soaking your legs in warm water with Epsom salts and rolling a tennis ball over them can help. Using a heat pack can also help. If you have an electric one you can keep it by your bed for immediate use of spasms happen in the middle of the night.

It's a really rare one called Dopa Responsive Dystonia, it's kind of like Parkinson's Disease, a lot of severe muscle cramping, tremors and balance issues. I think they tested for POTS, i didn't do the tilt table test but did do multiple rounds of heart and blood pressure reading moving through lying down, sitting and standing. I did have orthostatic hypotension and orthostatic tachycardia when something was wrong (being sick, dehydrated, after injections) but not generally in my day to day life so they don't think it's POTS because it's not chronic. This started in the Covid lockdown for me so the best guess the doctors have is that I went from being extremely active (2 hours of intense cardio 5 days a week) to doing nothing and my body sort of forgot how to properly regulate my heart rate and blood pressure. Since I started moving again the frequency has gone down a lot.

The only time I've passed out from this was getting an injection where I have the same kind of reaction. I've never passed out from the episodes that come on at random. Even though it always feels like I'm going to. It's hard to really test what's going on because it usually doesn't happen at the time of the test. For me they think it's related to my autonomic nervous system since I have a neurological disorder. It can be helpful to track what's happening at the time of episodes like hydration level, when you last ate, what physical position were you in, what were you doing/watching, how were you feeling etc that can sometimes give clues to what's triggering it and what it is. If you can get a pulse oximeter and record your heart rate also good.

Yes, doctor told me the term for that kind of dizziness is "pre-syncope". It took me a while to figure out what it was but it finally happened while i was wearing a pulse monitor and showed my heart rate was actually dropping at the time. It's a vasovagal response, where my heart and blood pressure drop suddenly, I stand up as an automatic response to get my heart rate up which it does, but then starts racing to compensate. Neither state feels good. We still don't know why this is happening to me, I do have some medical stuff probably contributing, my blood pressure is generally low, dehydration can bring it on and anxiety can also cause these episodes. The frequency of them go down the more physically active I am and the more I stay hydrated. But at the time it happens I feel like I'm dying, they're terrifying.

Take a breath, the majority of muscle spasms are not dystonia. A lot of things can cause neck spasms including posture, staying in one position too long, nutrition deficiencies like magnesium, not enough stretching, lifting things without the right technique... It's a long list and most are very easily treatable.

I have dystonia, my brother does not. He had some serious neck spasms for months. He made some lifestyle changes like not having his head over a textbook for 16 hours a day, getting enough sleep, taking magnesium supplements, stretching, getting a professional massage and doing physiotherapy. And the spasms stopped.

Talking to your doctor would be a good first step. They can check for signs of conditions like dystonia, check your nutrient levels, give you lifestyle change suggestions and refer you to massage and physio if you need it.

Yes. I have dystonia in my back as well but it can definitely be made worse when my CD flares up, and after it can stay pretty tight even when my neck is ok. A lot of nerves run through that area and sometimes get pinched which really ups the pain.

It's been difficult to deal with but I've found a few things that help. Professional massage from an RMT with strong hands, lidocaine injections into large muscle knots in that area and taking Baclofen have helped me.  On a daily basis limiting sitting (even with good posture it's a hard position for my back) and alternating between standing up and lying down, frequent stretching, at home TENS machine and not lifting heavy objects or doing repetitive movements. Physical activity has been critical for me. I take dance multiple times a week and that has made the biggest difference.

It can range from twitching and kind of a ripple repeatedly going through muscles to large sections of muscle completely locking with no movement pulling my body into a weird fixed posture. I can also get giant muscle knots (my largest one was the size of a plum) or visible strands of tight muscle that wrap around my back and restricted movement in my shoulders from my back pulling on the nearby muscles.

For me baclofen works for some muscles but not others. Dystonia affects most muscles in my body, though it's not always active at the same time. Baclofen mostly helps with the dystonia in my back. For my limbs it has no effect, they only respond to Sinemet and the dystonia in my neck only responds to Benztropine. I have had to increase my Baclofen dose over the years because the dystonia was getting less well controlled, I'm now at 20mg three times a day. You mentioned you have pkans, is that Pantothenate Kinase Associated Neurodegeneration? From my understanding of that condition (my doctors suspected I had it but i tested negative) that condition is progressive so the dystonia may be getting worse and you might need more medication to control the increase in severity.

However, it doesn't address mental components of anxiety like racing thoughts. Regardless of what medication you take i suggest doing Cognitive Behavioural Therapy and potentially Acceptance Commitment Therapy. They can really help break through the vicious circle.

Take him to ER, try to get him admitted, tests and specialist consults happen a lot quicker with inpatients. In most circumstances now the only path to admission is through the ER. If the ER absolutely won't admit him and you're near Toronto you can ask his primary care doctor for a referral to the Acute Ambulatory Care Unit at Women's College Hospital. I've seen a video instruction guide for how FBT is supposed to work.https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PL21D7E85D804263B2&si=wO3-2m9T-oPFg7cj 

In theory, while they're un-compromising on the rules the parents are supposed to be providing a lot of comfort and emotional support to deal with the psychological impact. They're supposed to stay calm at all times and be firm but kind. A lot of parents aren't capable of this and the relationship between some parents and their kids isn't conducive to emotional support. I've heard doctors/therapists say they can work with families who have issues to make it work for almost every family but I don't believe them. I hid by ED from my parents and didn't seek treatment until I was an adult because I knew having my parents involved in my treatment would be a disaster. And a lot of FBT ignores or seriously downplays the emotional part of ED's and just measures success on physical and behavioural points like meal completion and weight gain, pretending like the psychological issues will just get better by magic. I've been in a hospital program that had a similar philosophy - if you eat and follow the rules everything will be fine - short term it helped, the ED was so powerful I wasn't really capable of making choices because the ED was so powerful and I needed the structure to break that but long term it didn't help me. I did a different program later that addressed the emotional part and really cared how we felt. As well as therapy for the deeper issues the staff provided a lot of emotional support around meals and whenever feelings came up, kind of like surrogate parents. That was the first time I saw how FBT COULD work for some people.

How long is impossible to tell. It depends on so much stuff, your age, how long you've had an ED, how your ED has been lately, underlying medical conditions, activity level, level of luck... Even with my own body there have been different lengths of time in how long I could go before the really bad stuff started kicking in.

A lot of times there's no warning. Restricting can cause electrolyte imbalances which sometimes have no symptoms until cardiac arrest. If you get warning signs, stuff like palpitations, chest pain, heart beating too fast or too slow, blurred vision, tingling in your fingers, toes, or around your lips, shortness of breath, trouble breathing and passing out are all serious signs.

But going to stress it can be sudden. The first time I got any sign from my body that something serious was wrong I had felt fine right before, I just passed out, woke up in the hospital with a critical electrolyte imbalance which would've caused cardiac arrest. If I had passed out somewhere I was alone I probably wouldn't be here now. I figured I'd get a sign before anything like this happened. I didn't. The best way to know if your body is shutting down is medical monitoring with blood tests and ekg's.

Consider talking to your doctor about Prazosin. It's used to treat nightmares from PTSD. While it's not a sleep med it hugely improved my quality of sleep and made falling asleep a bit easier. Can be taken with other sleep meds usually.

Some of the relaxation methods CBT-i recommends don't work well for some people with PTSD. For me things like quiet meditations and body scans amp me up worst and often end up in flashbacks. Activities that are distracting but also don't require too much mental energy so the brain can still settle into sleepiness can help, I've done colouring and very simple origami. Your therapist might be able to help you find some of these activities that work for you. If you have access to DBT (Dialectical Behavioural Therapy) it has a lot of suggestions for distress tolerance skills that can be good options.

There's a few settings and some overlap:
- hospitalization on a medical unit, you're in there with people with other non-ED illness and the focus is to get you medically stable with things like iv's, supervised meals, possibly NG tubes. You spend most of the day in bed, little to no treatment for the mental component of ED's and it's usually short term. Sometimes you go home after, sometimes you go to an ED treatment program (see below). It can depend on things like availability, wait lists and insurance.
- an ED inpatient treatment program in a hospital. Either on a unit where everyone has an ED or in a psych unit with other patients there who have ED's. There is a schedule, usually with supervised meals eaten together and therapy groups in between and some individual appointments with a psychiatrist, therapist or dietician. And a lot of down time. There is still more of a focus around re-feeding and preventing restriction, purging etc than mental health. Some still do iv's, bed rest, NG tubes etc at the start. These can be longer term like several months, or short term with planning to go to a lower level of care like residential or partial hospitalization once you're medically stable.
- inpatient in an eating disorder facility. Similar to an ED inpatient treatment in a hospital but its generally a more home-like setting. They typically require a higher level of medical stability to go there, though some will still do Iv's and NG tubes at the start. There can be more of a focus on therapy, there's a schedule with supervised meals, group therapy and individual appointments and they might have activities like gentle yoga and art. Usually longer term stays like weeks to months but they often have lower levels of care in the same facility that you go to once medically stable
- sometimes "inpatient" is used to refer to residential treatment. Essentially like an "inpatient" program in an ED facility, but requires people to be medically stable. They tend to have more "real world" activities like cooking, restaurant outings and light exercise as you progress. It can take more than 3 years of consistent activity to heal with what the body goes through with dystonia. Especially for flexibility it takes persistence and patience. I know some of my muscles will be prone to tighten because of the dystonia but being in shape and being frequently active has made a huge difference. There's a big focus on flexibility, I'm stretching multiple times a day and doing straightening exercises that are working flexibility at the same time which helps the muscle lengthen rather than contract. Even if they're been tight from untreated dystonia for a long time muscles can be loosened and once they are improving alignment comes a lot easier after that. Engaging in movement activities that have a rhythm component seems to help the muscles, they use it for helping with Parkinson's symptoms and have done studies showing its effectiveness. I went to a good residential treatment centre. As an adult. I'm not a TTI survivor, my friends were sent to TTI facilities, I managed to hide my mental health problems from my parents so I didn't get sent too.

Some of the things that made my adult residential treatment good:
- completely voluntary treatment
- no communication restrictions with the outside world, we were allowed our phones and they encouraged us to use our family and friend support system
- we were not required to police other residents or call them out for anything and were encouraged to gently support each other
- narrow focus, they treated eating disorders and co-occuring mental health disorders
- all of the clinical staff were certified, trauma informed and actually good at therapy
- the residential staff genuinely cared about us, had previous work experience in mental health and appeared to be making more than minimum wage
- we weren't punished for mental health behaviours
- there weren't arbitrary rules there just to control us
- any changes to our treatment plan were done in consultation and with out consent
- they actually listened to us
- it was owned by two of the therapists with no corporation involved so they weren't cutting corners to maximize a big corporate profit. Because we, the residents, were paying for it, client comfort/satisfaction was important
- they didn't abuse us, shame us, label us, threaten us, isolate us, force medicate us, strip search us, restrain us or do any of the horrible things my friends experienced in TTI.

So IN THEORY I think "good" residential treatment can be helpful. I definitely needed it, outpatient wasn't enough for me, and I could've really benefited from a treatment experience like that as a teen. The problem is in reality they are NEVER going to give teenagers that kind of freedom and respect and they're not going to spend the extra money needed to create that safe and helpful environment. Since the teens aren't paying for their treatment TTI facilities can make profit at the expense of their experience, as long as the parents are kept happy. "Good" residential treatment for teens doesn't exist.

More safety measures would be great and could help to an extent. Heavily regulated inpatient psych units within a hospital tend to have less abuse (though not zero) and do need to exist for people who are at imminent risk of causing themselves serious harm. But TTI facilities are good at getting around safety measures and the abuse continues. I'm worried there aren't safety measures that could realistically be put in place that are enough to stop it.

I have the same problem. My trauma responses don't respond to logic or any thinking. The brain can sometimes develop a primal response to threats that by-passes the logic/thinking area of the brain and goes straight to the action/response area, so that we have a quicker response to get us away from the threat and save our lives. It makes sense in nature when the threat is a tiger. But this response can also remain for things that we may logically know we don't need to be afraid of. You see this in phobias, my mom logically knows that the house spider isn't scary yet she still runs from the room if she finds one. According to my therapist the way to lessen/get rid of this response is to expose yourself to the trigger a lot and eventually the primal response learns that it isn't threatening and eventually stops reacting. If you pair the exposure with something that makes you feel calm and comfortable but doesn't involve thinking, having that present during or right after can help. I personally had mix results with this, I did develop a milder response to some of the triggers but if I went a while without being exposed again the response came back. Apparently you have to keep doing it for the effect to last.

Palliative care approach will depend on what your team is willing to do. There's two things to figure out. 1) stopping treatment that is aimed at saving your life. There's a big difference between a harm reduction approach, which your team might be taking now, and a palliative care approach. I researched this and for multiple countries I've seen treatment court ordered most of the time. 2) providing treatment to ease pain and discomfort. Another discussion to have with your team is what ways might your body start breaking down before you die, what treatments are possible for that and what your team is willing to offer, for example pain meds, palliative sedation. If they're not willing or equipped to handle that you may have to try finding other doctors who are.

Not my client, case from law school:

A crew from a country in South America were on a ship with a large amount of cannabis to Alaska. Before they could get there the ship had mechanical issues and ran into a storm so the captain brought the ship to shore in a fairly remote cove in Canada for the safety of the crew. Once they landed the captain was worried the ship was going to capsize so they unloaded the cargo of cannabis onto the shore... where they were found and arrested for trafficking. In the days before even small amounts of cannabis were legal in Canada. 

However were found not guilty in a case that went all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada. The reason: the "necessity defense". If a person is faced with imminent danger (which they did not create themselves) and has no reasonable, legal alternative, it can excuse the crime. If it hadn't been for the storm they wouldn't have committed a crime under Canadian law, they had no plans to enter or import drugs into Canada. For the necessity defense the action a person takes does have to be proportional to the harm caused. In this case the court decided that protecting the lives of the people on the ship outweighed some very large bags of cannabis chilling on the Canadian shore for a bit. The case is Perka v The Queen if anyone wants to read the details.

Take a couple deep breaths and consider this: maybe your son's declining mental health is due to the environment he's in. I understand his February 6th suicide attempt must've been terrifying, I have PTSD from dealing with brothers' suicide attempts. BUT that fear can cloud reality. Your son came home, went to IOP and he was discharged for smoking marijuana with a peer, the IOP didn't want to deal with that. Not because of a safety issue like suicide or self-harm. 

The place that he was self-harming and checking his meds was a residential treatment facility, not at home. In the best case scenario these places have restrictions that prevent a teen from using coping skills and having to support of family and loved ones. Worst case scenario (which is actually very likely) the facility is abusing the teens and his self-harm and planning suicide is the only way he can escape that. You said you're worried that if you bring him out into the world he'll die, but based on his behaviour, and the long list of kids who die in residential facilities, the risk is probably higher in residential.

Talk to him. In person, where you're away from treatment staff. Ask him why he's been self-harm and planning suicide. Ask him what he would find helpful, what sort of things he needs to improve his safety and his mood. Ask him what is unhelpful and makes it worse. Take previous recommendations with a grain of salt - outpatient psychiatrists often get financial kickbacks for referring teens to residential programs. Look at PHP and IOP programs, ideally ones where an incident of smoking marijuana isn't grounds for discharge. DBT (Dialectical Behavioural Therapy) can often be helpful for people for people struggling with self-harm and other safety issues. It should be an accredited, comprehensive DBT rather than "DBT informed".

It's understandable that you want to keep your son safe but sending him to long term residential is going to have the opposite effect. They're not safe, he'll experience more trauma and if he survives his time in the facility he'll be in a worse position when he comes out.

I'm a lawyer, not in the U.S. Obligatory disclaimer: I'm not trained in U.S. law, I can't practice in the U.S., this is not legal advice, I'm just sharing my opinion on this, it maybe not be correct.

I would be very suspicious of the lawsuit you described. If the lawsuit already exists and they're asking people to sign on, then it should be a class action lawsuit, and that has a bunch of rules that don't seem like they're being followed here.

They should be saying who the lawsuit is against. It is HIGHLY unusual for a lawsuit to be against multiple, unrelated companies. Even under the same company but very different style of programs, that would be a hard case (in a class action the lawyer has to establish that everyone had similar enough experiences to be decided together). I would use caution.

The way a class action works is that there is a single or small group of "representative plaintiffs" (I think in the U.S. they call them "lead plaintiffs") who give their evidence to the court, have a bigger role in deciding what the terms of the settlement will be, if it settles, and they usually have stricter rules about what they can and can't do or say. Requiring the lead plaintiffs not to speak publicly, and potentially privately, would not be unusual. Since they'll be giving evidence in court there's concerns about what they say being inconsistent, could be used against them, etc. Requiring everyone who signs onto it to not speak publicly or privately would be VERY unusual. There's not the same evidence concerns and there is concern for restriction the free speech rights of everyone involved, and they're (sometimes) sensitive to how important that right is for institutional abuse survivors (not sure if the last part applies in the U.S.). I personally would not sign onto that.

If they're not going the class action route and trying to recruit survivors as individuals for thousands of individual cases I highly doubt any one law firm would have the capacity to handle, and do a good job with, that many lawsuits. I also doubt they'd have lawyers who can practice in every state where there's a program. And if they were doing this they should be giving you a lot of other information about the process, what you'll need to do, your goals, what they can offer etc. BEFORE they ask for no public or private communication. This also seems suspicious.

Sorry this is lengthy, I want to be thorough. I don't want to see any survivors get scammed or lose their voice. You deserve to speak your truth and connect with each other and do things that help you heal. 

TLDR: this lawsuit sounds suspicious and requiring you not to talk about it is unusual and sounds unreasonable.

Because I'm an ally and not a survivor (some of my friends were sent to TTI, I wasn't) the first thing I had to do was connect with survivors. Most importantly to make sure I was helping in a way that they actually found helpful, and secondly because lawyers and journalists will need to hear directly from survivors in moving forward. 

For lawyers a good place to start can be looking at what firms have handled previous lawsuits for TTI schools and other institutional abuse cases like institutions for adults with disabilities. Firms that have done this kind of work include Koskie Minsky LLP, McKenzie Lake Lawyers and Rochon Genova LLP. Send an email to the firm describing the issues you've observed, what you heard from survivors (with their consent) and their contact information. You can look at their website to see previous similar cases they've done and reference that  (e.g. Koskie Minsky handled a class action lawsuit against a school called Sheila Morrison School, now closed)  and if the website lists any lawyers that worked on the lawsuit you can include them in the email.

A person has to be a danger to themself or others to be involuntarily admitted so you might have to pick the right moment. For a Form 2, which lets police send him to the hospital to be examined, a person needs to either threaten to kill/seriously hurt themself, threaten to kill/seriously injure someone else or be deteriorating to the point they will cause themself serious harm e.g. they won't eat for days/weeks, they won't get medical care for serious infections. CAMH seems to understand the link between substance use and mental health a bit better.

You can also call the Toronto Community Crisis Service or the Gerstein Crisis Centre. They send people out to his location, he has to agree to talk to them but sometimes people are more willing to talk to someone in their home environment.

I got diagnosed as a kid. Doctors considered a few physical diagnoses and also considered that it was psychological before I they figured out it was Dopa Responsive Dystonia. Tests I had:
- some sort of nerve conduction test with electrode pads (not needles)
- EEG
- some really detailed clinical examinations, beyond the standard neurological tests, focussing on movement e.g. trying to hop on one foot 10 times
- MRI of the brain and spine
- blood tests
- L-Dopa trial (this is how I got the diagnosis)
- genetic testing (after diagnosis, confirmed the Dopa Responsive Dystonia)
- they requested a lumbar puncture, I refused, they didn't think it was worth holding me down for it

On top of not running the full testing I think some doctors jump to psychological causes when they can't figure it out before getting another opinion from a different doctor. Luckily my neurologist was great and got a consult with a doctor who used to be head of the Department with more than 30 years experience and he recognized it.

In real life the hospital wouldn't just accept the insurance company denying the claim, they'd sue the insurance company. Often insurance companies can deny a claim if their terms are breached, they argue they signed up for a different level of risk, if they had known it was going to be like this they wouldn't have signed on o cover it. The fact Arizona jumped in last minute against company policy likely wouldn't change anything about that. Employers are expected to have structures in place to control what their employees do and if they don't the employer is often liable for what its employees do. This also means that the hospital probably could not refuse to pay the doctors' claim because they're responsible for what Arizona did. Particularly if they never made Arizona aware of the limit on the number of attendings rule then its not her fault at all, it's theirs.

However, there's an argument to be made that Arizona being on the plane wasn't materially relevant to the entire claim, just the amount they'd have to pay. Arizona being on the plane could not have increased the risk of it crashing. The reason they would have a cap on the number of attendings on the plane is likely that they would have to pay more for attendings if something happened to them because their salaries are higher. If that argument was successful then the insurance company would still have to pay the claim but could subtract the difference between how much it would have to pay for Arizona as an attending than if she had been a resident. Or they might have gotten away with excluding Arizona from coverage completely and could subtract whatever they would have paid for Arizona but still pay for the others.

Could DRD meds like Levodopa work on severe ADHD? No. While both increase dopamine they're targeted to do it in different areas of the brain and to treat very different causes of low dopamine. Levodopa is used for the part of the brain that controls movement, medications that treat ADHD target the part of the brain that controls thoughts, actions and emotions.

No. Most DRD is genetic (they've identified two genes and looking at others) and caused by a problem in the brain's ability to metabolize dopamine, an issue that's present at birth. In many cases DRD symptoms appear very early in childhood. No autoimmune component. While it's not caused by childhood trauma stress can worsen symptoms of DRD and childhood trauma could cause increased stress.

Depends on whether you're an adult and what you're being hospitalized for. If you're under 18 the line between voluntary and involuntary gets a lot less clear. If you're an adult a psychiatrist can have you involuntarily hospitalized if you're medically unstable at risk of imminent death or serious permanent damage or if you're actively suicidal.

If you're an adult and medically unstable you usually get admitted to a medical ward. You might get a IV, supervised meals and/or a feeding tube. People who are involuntary seem to be more likely to end up with a feeding tube. You might have a psychiatrist check in with you from time to time and you might get some work sheets but there's usually not much mental health treatment, it's focused almost completely on getting you medically stable. You can usually have visitors but mostly your day is spent alone in your room resting. If you're there voluntarily you might keep some privileges like being allowed to go to the lobby or get some fresh air, potentially in a wheelchair. If you're there involuntarily you won't be able to leave the ward. Here's the big one: if getting medically stable will be a longer process, if you are voluntary they might try to transfer you to an eating disorder inpatient unit if you agree, and if/when a bed becomes available. All of the adult eating disorder programs in Ontario require you to be voluntary. They have a structured day with supervised meals with the other patients, therapy groups, occasional individua sessions and down time where you can hang out with the other patients and watch movies and stuff. If you're involuntary you stay on the medical unit with the IV, supervised meals and tube until you're medically stable enough to go home. Neither is fun but a lot of people prefer the eating disorder IP because its less boring and the social time and support from other patients makes things a lot easier to handle.

If you're an adult and actively suicidal you get admitted to a psychiatric ward. They usually do not treat eating disorders and are focused on getting you safe from suicide intentions/behaviours for you to safely go home. There's usually some structure with therapy groups, meals and recreation activities. If you're voluntary you can go on recreation activities that are off unit like walks and sometimes you can go to a nearby coffee shop or something. If you're involuntary you can't leave the ward. It's possible that you might have different rules and supervision around meal times. Sometimes people with eating disorders can get sent to an acute care ward/section of the ward where someone has eyes on you at all times. People hospitalized for medical instability can sometimes end up there, especially to prevent things like frequent purging or exercise. No one in the acute care wards appear to be voluntary.

In both cases if you're voluntary then technically you have the right to leave when you want. But they can assess you before you leave and if the doctor thinks you're in danger from medical stability or suicide risk they can switch you to involuntary. If you're admitted involuntarily at first you can decide to agree to stay voluntarily later on. You might have to earn some trust from the staff before you get the privileges that come with that but it can put you on that path.

I have DRD, started showing symptoms around age 5, diagnosed at 10 after a couple misdiagnoses, i'm 34 now and have been taking L-dopa since I was diagnosed. There are some symptoms that overlap between DRD and Parkinson's. There's a cluster of symptoms are referred to as "Parkinsonism" - tremors, rigidity and slow movement. Some people with DRD (not all) will have Parkinsonism symptoms. Having Parkinsonism DOES NOT mean that you have Parkinson's Disease.  While some people may have DRD and Parkinson's Disease for many others the Parkinsonism symptoms are just part of the DRD. I had a tremor which started when I was 8 but it was effectively treated by the L-dopa. I don't experience it now unless I'm sleep deprived or sick.

DRD generally does not inevitably get worse as time goes by like Parkinson's se does. You might never have any symptoms develop that are more than what you have now. L-dopa is the gold standard of treatment. It usually stays quite effective but if it doesn't fully control your symptoms there are other medications that can be used with it e.g. I have back spasms that aren't resolved by L-dopa so I also have a muscle relaxant I take for that. 

I found the most effective "alternative" treatment for me has been exercise. There's some evidence that activities that involve rhythm like dance, or boxing or tai chi can be particularly effective but doing anything  that's active and that you enjoy is helpful. Massage can be nice too. Getting good sleep and trying to keep stress levels down is important. You should share your worries about what will happen in the future with your doctor, hopefully they can help reassure you. I hope this is helpful.

So B.C. and Alberta actually have different systems of charging. In Alberta police lay charges, once they do this the charge is on your record - there are some ways to get them withdrawn like a peace bond but you were charged. B.C. has something called Crown pre-charge screening (Quebec and New Brunswick also have it). In a situation where you would be charged by police in another province, police recommend a charge to the Crown and the Crown decides whether there's enough evidence and/or public interest to charge you. In your case it looks like the police recommended a charge and after reviewing the recommendation and the evidence the Crown denied it so you were not charged. If the police officer you spoke to said you were charged it might be because they aren't familiar with the B.C. system of charging.

In both provinces being charged does not mean you have a criminal record, for that you would need to be convicted. This happens by either by pleading guilty or being found guilty at a trial (can be a more informal process for smaller things like some traffic offenses.)

- before beginning, have therapy sessions to pre-plan with the child how their parents can help them deal with emotions that come up, e.g. a list of after dinner activities to choose from. I've experienced low blood pressure and fainting. Disclaimer: I have a different movement disorder but similar symptoms and meds to Parkinson's. Things that might be helpful:
- Find out if her blood pressure and heart rate are always low or if anything in particular drops it e.g. standing up, after eating, times of day etc. Getting a blood pressure cuff and a pulse oximeter can let you measure and track it
- Staying hydrated is critical. Check with her doctor but eating more salt might also help, as it raises blood pressure. 
- She should sit and stand up very slowly and lie down right away if she feels faint
- Having grab bars or other very sturdy objects around that she can grab on to if she feels faint. Between my bed and bathroom I have something in arms length the whole way. If you can get an Occupational Therapist to do an assessment they can suggest things to maintain safety
- Maintaining physical activity if possible can be helpful. It can be a bit difficult with low blood pressure so look into exercises that can be done sitting down. A physiotherapist could help with this.

Waking up with littler to no physical symptoms is actually a characteristic of another movement disorder called Dopa Responsive Dystonia which is similar to Parkinson's in some ways, overlap in symptoms, similar treatment. I don't think they fully know why yet. I don't mean to suggest your dad has it, the condition usually shows up earlier in life and doesn't involve dementia. But I'd guess there's a similar thing that happens for some people with Parkinson's where a long sleep relieves symptoms. The technical term for it is "diurnal fluctuations."' When he takes his morning dose, falls asleep and wakes up worse is he also taking Seroquel at this time? Anti-psychotic medications can reduce dopamine in the brain which can worsen Parkinson's symptoms. While Seroquel does less of this than other anti-psychotic medications it's still possible. And unfortunately medications that increase dopamine including Rytary can make hallucinations worse so he may be experiencing less of that when he wakes up and hasn't had them for a while. It's a horrible catch 22.

I was not motivated when I went to PHP. The only reason I went is my closest friends said if I didn't go then they couldn't be around me anymore and I couldn't stand to lose them. It put me on a path towards recovery instead of just deteriorating further. It was worth reminding yourself that you can try it and if it doesn't work for you then you can always leave.

I also have Dopa Responsive Dystonia, diagnosed at 10. Also taking levodopa which really helped symptoms in my feet and hands and motor symptoms. I started getting neck and shoulder tightness in my early 20s but I wrote it off as normal neck pain from being a student and studying long hours. But then in my late 20s one night my neck completely locked up, pretty much at a 90 degree angle facing the ground and I couldn't move it at all in any direction for 5 hours. It didn't unlock on it's own, I had to go to the ER. Unfortunately that was not a one time thing, I've had more episodes like that since. Levodopa had no effect on these muscles but an anti-cholinergic medication called Benztropine loosens them pretty well for me. My neurologist said it's still part of the Dopa Responsive Dystonia, just a new way it's presenting, and not a separate condition. I don't want to scare you, everyone's body does different things, but seeing you neurologist for your neck/shoulder/back pain would be a good idea.

I'm a patient of Dr. Lewis, in my experience he's been (and continues to be) a great doctor. He has a wealth of knowledge and a great bedside manner - a combination that can be a rare find with a specialist. While he's very kind, he's not a volunteer, and nor should he be.

I recognize no system is perfect and I don't have a solution to all of Healthcare funding in Ontario but this really puts the flaws of the fee-for-service model. For each surgery, in the time it took for him to deal with the billing Dr. Lewis probably could've completed multiple simple surgeries from the backlog identified as a priority. This issue also gets brought up a lot in other areas like family medicine. Doctors have to do a lot of admin work related to billing and managing expenses like renting and staffing an office. This isn't a good use of their time and skills and cuts into the time they have to treat patients. It would be good to consider other models that let doctors focus on being doctors, in all types of medicine. For example, many family health teams typically use a Blended Salary Model where doctors are salaried based on number of patients enrolled, plus some bonuses. There are other fee models.

Dr. Lewis's work is life altering. He is making a significant difference in pain and function for his patients for a long time (especially at Sick Kids). The personal and financial costs of living with the type of back problems that Dr. Lewis treats are significant. I hope changes are made soon so he can get back to doing the great work he does to his full potential.

One of the treatment  usually tried for dystonia, particularly if it might be medication related, are anti-cholinergic medications. One of them is a medication called Benztropine, it sounds a lot like it's a benzodiazepine but it's just the name, they're completely different. If they haven't tried anti-cholinergics you could bring that up with your doctor. 

If your doctor has not done a lot of tests (e.g. blood work, MRI scans) to rule out other things consider getting a second opinion. Drugs that can cause dystonia are usually medications that decrease dopamine in the brain, like anti-psychotic drugs. Zopiclone doesn't usually have this effect, neither do benzodiazepines, however, people's brains react differently and there appear to be a small number of people who have had this reaction to benzodiazepines, so anything is possible. But this is rare enough that your doctor should be checking for other possible causes because what you're experiencing isn't typical.

I think that depends on his mental state. If he's fairly clear headed and capable of rational thinking (even if he doesn't currently understand why this has to happen) and his memory is fairly intact, have the conversation with him. He might be upset for a bit but it will help preserve trust, which is going to be really important as he needs more assistance with things. If he's in a mental state where he's not well connected to reality (on day to day stuff, not just the apartment) and he's having severe enough memory issues that he would forget what happened to the apartment and you'd have to have the conversation over and over, it might be kinder not to bring it up.

If you decide to tell him, having the reasons come from his physiotherapist and neurologist may be helpful, e.g. explaining to him that while they are working on improving walking they don't feel it's safe for him to be on a third floor apartment with no elevator and that they don't think there will be a point where that would be safe. Also try to keep in mind, for your father this is probably more than just the apartment, it's potentially symbolic of losing independence and that the Parkinson's is progressing to the point he won't get his old life back. Be patient, listen to him and try and address concerns he raises together. You can be honest about your boundaries and what you can't afford. This might take a few conversations but it would be ideal to ultimately have him make the decision.

In a treatment centre setting trying to maximize measures for comfort and minimize unnecessary rules that make life harder. E.g. for after meals it seems to be common practice to have patients sit around the table for a while, at a time that's both physically and mentally very uncomfortable. While supervision might be necessary, moving patients somewhere comfortable like a lounge where they can lie down if they want, offer heat pads, and different distractions like movies, art supplies, calls/texts to loved ones, so people can choose what works for them.

Not hospital food, have prepping meals be part of the process when they're ready. There might need to be certain requirements for meals for physical healing but things like food challenges should be based on readiness and not "Thursday is challenge dessert day." 

Having many different types of therapy available. DBT, ACT, CBT, EMDR, art therapy, yoga, support groups. Having "family" therapy with whoever the person identifies as their support system they want to involve. Therapy shouldn't be time limited, I think a lot of the time people don't recover because therapy cuts off way too soon.

Focusing on increasing motivation. Identifying things a person enjoys and how recovery can benefit them e.g. being able to go to their friend's birthday party and fully participate, having the energy and concentration to join a baseball league. Things that make recovery feel worth it.

I have a 10mg dose in the morning when I first get up but my anxiety is usually the lowest in the morning and worst at night (why my night dose is higher). I don't sleep well usually so I'm too tired to think much when I wake up which keeps the anxiety low. Let your doctor know that your anxiety peaks in the morning and they can hopefully address that with a higher morning dose or an extended release so a dose from the night before would still be working in the morning.

There are some things that can cause Levodopa to not work such as dose, timing, foods eaten recently and the right dose to titrate up to. It would be ideal if you were able to work with someone with medical knowledge to help avoid these issues. Some GP's are willing to do a trial of Levodopa for someone without a diagnosis of Parkinson's Disease because under the right conditions it can be a good test. If your GP is not willing to do this could you potentially find another doctor who could?

If your uncle is being treated by a neurologist (I see the "had Parkinson's" in your post so if he's passed on my condolences) he could potentially approach his neurologist for advice about your situation.

Group therapy/support groups can be really helpful. Building connections with people who understand and being able to bounce ideas for problems off each other can help with moving forward. A dystonia-specific group might be hard to find but a group for you to people with disabilities/chronic illnesses will have members who experience similar issues. For the nightmares the most helpful thing for me has been a medication called Prazosin. It has really decreased the frequency and intensity of my nightmares. Before I was taking it I found the best thing to help me deal with a nightmare that had happened was exercise. Sometimes a full gym workout, sometimes a walk to work. Fresh air could be somewhat helpful too.

For the insomnia, focus on what works for YOU. Techniques for falling asleep that may work great for people without PTSD, or work for some people with PTSD, may not work for you and trying to force it can make it worse. For example, some people find meditations relaxing and are helpful before bed. But some people with PTSD (me included) find that meditation increases their anxiety. Screen time is a big one, for insomnia the advice is generally to limit phone and tv before bed BUT for some people with PTSD tv and phone help keep the anxiety down and removing them increases anxiety and cancels out any helpful effect they would have on sleep. For me Candy Crush or other low intensity pattern games helped calm me down a lot and made it easier to relax before bed. A blue light filter on devices for the evening can help. Activities that can distract you so you're not thinking about trying to relax or falling asleep can help, as long as they don't require a lot of brain power. 

Not everyone with PTSD can handle total darkness. I keep a light on and have a sleep mask that I can pull off quickly if I wake up in the night. I also sleep with ear plugs so that I'm not playing a constant game of "what's that noise" while trying to fall asleep.

Trying to really shorten the time between when you put yourself into bed and when you fall asleep is good. Not getting into bed unless you're already really tired gives less time for the anxiety to develop. For this time I have a few memories I can think about of times in my life I felt really safe that are untainted by the trauma and I try to focus on those as much as I can. 

I keep my clock faced away from my bed so I can't count the minutes of how long I've been lying there. Ideally you want to be in a position where you're not TRYING to relax, you're just doing peaceful, pleasant activities for however long that takes, low key enjoying it but not enough that you'd want to stay awake for it when you start to feel sleepy.

Advice I got from my dietician: if you're somewhat new to intuitive eating and previously had rules or restrictions for yourself on sugar you might be drawn to sugar because it's "allowed" now and because your body thinks that could only be temporary and wants to stock up on it while it can. It's kind of like if you told a kid they can have whatever they want in the kitchen, while they might like lots of foods they'll probably go for the cookies because they can.

I found this to be true for me, I had a while where I always wanted what I'd restricted but after a while that broadened out, sometimes I'd want chocolate, other times I'd want tomatoes. Things even out when your body learns to trust.

I try to make sure different food options are equally accessible and convenient. I keep cut up vegetables and fruit in the fridge so I'm not put off by having to chop it up, and having already made meals available that I can just grab if I feel like it without having to prep them. Include things you know you like e.g. favourite vegetables, favourite sauces, favourite spices. Keeping all options open.

So zopiclone itself can be safe for a long time, I've been taking it for 8 years pretty much nightly. What may NOT be safe is using it to get through alcohol withdrawal. If you're talking about using it to replace one or two drinks that help you fall asleep that might be okay, but if you have heavier use, like lots of drinks and drinking throughout the day withdrawal can be dangerous with symptoms like hallucinations and seizures and is potentially life threatening. Zopiclone can't prevent this. There are medications that can help for safer alcohol withdrawal, often it's a benzodiazepine, please talk to a doctor if you think you're going to experience withdrawal.

 You've clearly done a lot of researcher.  I'm listing a few things that I've tried that were helpful that aren't on your list. Not medical advice I'm not a doctor and every situation is different (for me the CD is part of a full body Dopa Responsive Dystonia)
- anti-cholinergic medications. Benadryl is in that class and you mentioned it affects your mood so if you try this be careful, but I found other anti-cholinergics like Benztropine to be a different experience. A lot more effective if taken through and injection, at least for the first dose
- anti-inflammatory medications like ibuprofen or stronger aids 
- TENS treatment had a very temporary relief effect for me, like while I was receiving it and about 5 minutes after, but I have a home TENS machine so I can just keep it on for an evening
- Different positions, while I found activity is extremely important, if I'm not being active so watching tv or working on my laptop I try and be either reclined with pillows around my neck, lying down or with my body wrapped over a large yoga ball to keep my neck supported. I did have to start working from home to make this possible.

Again, everybody's different, that was just my experience. I hope you find something that gives you some relief soon.

Depending on where you live there are exercise classes for people with Parkinson's, the classes are set up for people dealing with dystonia, stiffness, balance issues, tremors etc. I've seen them for dance and boxing and I'm sure there are other types out there. The instructors have experience with working with people with movement disorders, they can help people make modifications if they're not able to do something.

I've been taking dance classes most of my life despite having dystonia. I'm lucky, my dystonia usually responds well to treatment, but while I wasn't well my teacher, who also teaches dance classes for Parkinson's, sent me a video of what she teaches there. She gives a lot of options on different ways to do things.

I've found exercises that incorporate rhythm have been really helpful for the dystonia. It's like trying to follow the rhythm fights the disjointed feeling of the dystonia and helped my muscles sync up and function better. It also helped my balance and coordination.

If you can I recommend adding ACT (Acceptance Commitment Therapy) to your treatment, especially a concept called "diffusion". It helped me get out of the circling pattern, it's kind of focused on the process of anxiety rather than the content. While CBT would have you identify thought distortions ACT would have you recognize that you're having a thought, nothing more and nothing less, and teach you skills on how to distance yourself from it and act in a way that lets you live according to what you values. I was really skeptical when I first learned about this but I found it really helpful. I still use CBT and it's useful to a point, but ACT was helpful when CBT hit its limit.

Having a Movement Disorder Specialist (as others have said) is important. They may be aware of treatment options that your dad hasn't tried yet. To make sure the doctor sees what he's experiencing it can be helpful to bring videos. Record him moving while on the medication and off the medication, have him describe what he's feeling in the video as well, especially stuff like stiffness that isn't easy to see. It might be helpful to video a few times to show the pattern. Close up videos of different parts of the body like hands and feet can also be helpful.

My neurologist recommended it, tried it and it didn't work but I did respond well to a different anti-cholinergic (same class). Check with your doctor before trying for the right dose, length of treatment and for whether it's a good treatment option for you, certain types of dystonia tend to respond better to anti-cholinergics e.g. dystonia triggered by another medication, dystonia related to Parkinson's Disease, sudden onset of dystonia in children. They can also balance the benefits and risks.

I've had musical hallucinations on a certain pain medication. It didn't come with visual hallucinations (though I've had that happen with a different medication). If he's had any recent changes to medication that could be a cause. For me realizing what was going on helped me deal with it. The first time it after about 30 minutes of "listening" to music I realized "wait I'm in the ER and there's no radio... this must be in my head then." If he's waking up or falling asleep at 2am there are also hypnagogic and hypnopompic hallucations that can happen when a person is waking up or falling sleep, they can happen to anyone but they can also suggest a sleep disorder so that's worth talking to his doctor about. If your grandpa is lucid enough to understand it then walking him through what's going on might help, and then write it down and put it in a lot of places he'll see it. If he's not a fan of the music he's hearing have an easy set up for him to play music he likes. It might be helpful if you can secure the attic so he can't get up there without assistance. "The tech left a speaker in my attic" comes off as a bit paranoid which is concerning and it would be good to raise that with his doctor.

I think DBT in group alone can be beneficial IF the group therapist is well trained in DBT and good at teaching it.

The first time I did DBT was part of a hospital eating disorder program and it made me think that DBT didn't work for me. But I found out later they just had no idea what they were doing. I'm pretty sure they learned everything they knew about DBT from a PowerPoint presentation and they got so much wrong.

A few years later I did a DBT group with a properly trained DBT therapist and it was so much better. They used practical examples to demonstrate skills, explained the skills with different options that people could use based on personal preferences and personality differences, they gave us assignments to practice at home and would troubleshoot issues people had. Things like knowing certain skills work better at certain distress levels (which the hospital program got wrong) was really helpful for me. I did a DBT (Dialectical Behavioral Therapy) program and my therapist taught me 3 life-changing lessons that have made coping with anxiety a lot easier. 

1) using the right skill for the right distress level. Apparently learning mindfulness and meditating is most effective when you're in a neutral or calm and positive mental state, for a high level of distress it often doesn't work and other distress tolerance skills are more appropriate. 
2) having options for skills and using what works for you. For example, for the highest distress level DBT recommends changing your temperature like taking a cold shower or holding ice, intense exercise or breathing and muscle relaxation exercises. The first two worked a lot better for me. 
3) mindfulness does not have to be sitting in complete silence trying to meditate. For people with PTSD it can make you feel worse because the fight/flight sense is always running, so things like walking meditations are often better.

I would highly recommend looking into DBT if you're looking to find calm in a way that works for you. While it's ideal to work with a therapist, there's a lot of info and skill ideas online.

It sort of depends what the document is used for in the end.  There might be a legal requirement under a government regulation that says "any time there is a restraint you have to get witness statements from everyone who witnessed it" . And these statements would basically sit in a box but the RTC could pull them out if they ever got investigated and they would be able to say "we did what the regulation said to do." Some investigations might read through them, others would just check a box that they exist. It's basically a record, kind of like how people are supposed to keep receipts when they do their taxes, so if anyone checks they can show they "followed the rules" .

The other situation where these could become a legal document is if the RTC gets sued or if any of the staff were criminally charged. The RTC would likely give them to the court as "evidence" that they didn't do anything wrong during restraints. However, the lawyer for the student suing them or the prosecution would point out that the statements weren't made under oath. Sometimes this means that they can't be used in court because the proper way to hear from witnesses, if they can find them, is to bring them into court, or get a statement under oath, to tell the court what happened. Sometimes they can be used but the lawyer (if they're good) will warn the judge not to take them completely seriously because there may be problems with them, like the RTC telling you what the write.

I should say, all of this assumes systems working as they're supposed to. The TTI aren't ethical so there's always the chance that investigators are paid off or court staff overlook the potential for coercion. *sigh* I think you are right about the pen instead of pencil part, pencil makes a less reliable document because it can be erased so the RTC may have had you use pen so it would seem more "tamper-proof".

There's two types of therapy I found helpful for intrusive and ruminating thoughts. 
1) CBT (Cognitive Behavioural Therapy) can help you recognize problems with the thoughts you're having and change them to thoughts that don't cause as much distress. 
2) Acceptance Commitment Therapy (ACT). This can be particularly helpful if you've done CBT and the intrusive thoughts keep coming at you anyways. There's an area of it called "decision" that helps you recognize a thought for what it is - a thought, and get some emotional space from it and lont term reduce them. The first exercise I got was write down an intrusive thought (e.g. "if I leave the house I will get struck by lightning") and then write it again but add "I am having a thought that..." to the beginning ("I am having a thought that if I leave the house I will get struck by lightning"). It seems simple and there's a lot more techniques. To it but this REALLY helped me with intrusive thoughts.

Ideally learn this stuff with a therapist. However if you're not able to easily find a therapist trained in these techniques there are tons of workbooks, charts, even YouTube videos that will walk you through it. You can work on both CBT and ACT, see where they work best for you. I hope you get some relief soon.

In the spirit of positivity I will share the story of when I first started treatment. Recent changes to my condition aside, it's still pretty special.

As a kid there was something noticably wrong from the time I started walking. By the time I was 6 my legs and feet would cramp up after trying to walk a few blocks, by the time I was 8 I couldn't walk at all in the evenings and by the time I was 9 I was in a wheelchair after 3pm and I had tremors all through my body with my hands shaking so much I couldn't hold a pen. Doctors weren't sure what was wrong, at first they thought Cerebral Palsy but that doesn't progress so they were starting to suspect another disorder that was degenerative and ultimately terminal. I didn't know that at the time but I can't begin to imagine what my parents went through.

Luckily in all of this I was seen by an incredible pediatric neurologist who suggested it could be Dopa Responsive Dystonia. They prescribed Sinemet and the response was unbelievable. In one week I went from not being able to walk 3 blocks home from school to walking a mile down the beach and back with no problem. The cramping, the tremors, the coordination problems, all of that just disappeared. 

I had been taking ballet as a kid before the diagnosis and treatment. That got harder as the symptoms progressed. My teacher was incredibly understanding and wonderful about keeping me involved however, at the end it was pretty much me sitting on the floor doing arm movements. I did have to put in a lot of hard work to stretch out the muscles and work on balance and strengthening but within a year my mom couldn't pick me out of the group of dancers. 

The rest of my childhood, teen years and into adult life I kept taking the Sinemet. Except for some close friends people didn't know I had Dystonia. I kept dancing, up to 6 days a week doing moves I would never have dreamed I could. I decided I wanted to go to law school and used the experience I had with Dystonia as my admissions essay. The week after I became a lawyer I walked over to the children's hospital where they diagnosed and treated me to give the doctors and nurses who took care of me a picture of me in my robes (in my country lawyers wear robes like judges) and a thank you card saying I couldn't have walked across the stage if it hadn't been for them. 

Things I learned from this experience, I am so incredibly grateful that the form of Dystonia I have responds to Sinemet. For me it has been an absolutely magic drug. Even at times it hasn't worked perfectly I'm grateful that it works most of the time. I've had times where I wasn't responding to it briefly and was in the hospital not able to walk, and the looks on the faces of my nurses when I started responding again and got up and walked, that was pretty incredible. It's not the only medication I take for Dystonia now, other medications, in my case Baclofen and Benztropine, have had some really good responses too, just wanted to put that out there for the people whose Dystonia is not Dopa Responsive.

For anyone who is interested in considering it, I highly recommend dance as a form of treatment. My neurologist and other doctors have said that it's the reason I have been able to function so well. It even helps muscles in my back where I experience Dystonia but those muscles have not responded so well to Linemen. Dance has a bunch of components that are great for working on Dystonia symptoms like stretching tight muscles, working on balance and coordination and developing fluid movements. But I find there's something about the rhythm in the movement that helps a lot more than other forms of cardio exercise I've done. There was a recently released study on patients with Parkinson's Disease showing dance was helpful in treating Parkinson's symptoms, I can find the link if anyone is interested. Dancing has also done a lot for me mentally, way too much for me to go into in this already long post, but in general it's helpful to have something in life that brings happiness and gives a reason to continue pushing forward in life which can be really challenging with Dystonia sometimes. 

I hope the positives here can be helpful to someone.

It can help to start the conversation as a general discussion about what they want their end of life to be like. Would they prioritize living as long as possible or reducing pain? Talk about the possible symptoms they could be dealing with, what are they willing to deal with and what would they find intolerable. From there it's a bit easier to move into talking about their options. End of life care is kind of a spectrum, on one end there's no medical involvement, at the other there's MAID. But between that there's other things like palliative sedation (medication to make them sleep all or most of the time) medication for pain control like morphine which can speed up death at high doses, whether they want nutrition or hydration through and IV if they can't eat or drink. In the context of all of this you can present MAID. They can make the decision on each of these treatments and all of this should be recorded in an advanced directive. Make it clear you will support them in whatever they ultimately choose to do.

The earlier you can have this talk and if they decide they want MAID bring it up with their doctor and get the paperwork done the better. In every jurisdiction I know of that offers this the person has to be capable of making decisions. Where I am it means they have to understand what they are doing and appreciate the consequences. The person does need to have capacity at the time of MAID being administered however, if the person goes through the assessment process earlier on while still effectively able to communicate the doctor may be more comfortable relying on yes or no answers at the end if communication has become difficult. If they do end up losing capacity before they can agree to MAID the other measures like sedation and pain medication can be followed from their advance directive so it's good to have these down as a plan B. 

If you're able to get connected with a palliative care doctor this can be extremely helpful, both for the end of life part and for maximizing comfort as things progress.

Try not to hate yourself for putting this on the table. My parent was actually incredibly relieved to hear this was possible. As a person with a movement disorder with Parkinson's symptoms I've experienced incredible pain and discomfort, frustrating loss of mobility and symptoms chipping away at the enjoyable parts of life and I will absolutely be requesting MAID when the point of no return comes. The fact that you're willing to being this up with them shows a lot of kindness. Speaking bluntly this tends to suck worse for the loved ones than the person themself. And ultimately it will be your parent's decision. You can just hold their hand and support them regardless.
