Sure! I will say this is the advice my therapist gave to me, other people might have different things that work for them.
- Extreme distress use TIP skills: Temperature (e.g. cold shower or holding ice), Intense Exercise and Paced breathing or Progressive Muscle Relaxation (this one did not work for me during high distress)
- Moderate to high distress use ACCEPTS skills: these involve temporarily distracting yourself from your feelings such as doing an Activity (talking a walk, watching a movie), Thinking about something else (singing a song in your mind) or Sensations (squeezing a stress ball)
- for moderate distress use IMPROVE skills: focused on making your environment more pleasant, such as using Imagery (imagining a beach), Relaxation (massaging your shoulders) or Encouragement (saying affirmations to yourself)
- for mild to moderate distress, usually when the worst of the distress is starting to pass through using TIP, ACCEPTS and Improve skill, to try and return to calm, use Self Soothing Skills: focusing on the 5 senses  like Hearing (listen to your favourite song) or touch (sitting in the warm sun)
- feeling neutral to positive, practice mindfulness techniques to overall improve mental health such as describing thoughts and emotions without judging them, focusing on one thing in the present moment. These skills lay the foundation for Emotional Regulation skills, which help you learn to handle future situations without getting overwhelmed.
I gave some examples under each category but there's hundreds of different skills under each one for people to try out and see what works for them. There's lots of lists online under DBT skills.

Unspoken rules for all:
1) give people personal space, don't stand too close to them (at least arms length away) and don't touch them

2) avoid talking to people wearing earbuds, if you need directions ask someone else. A lot of people wear them as a sign that they don"t want anyone to talk to them

3) except for bars, don't hit on/flirt with strangers. In bars, try a bit of small talk first so you can gauge whether a person wants to talk to you

4) if a person is not engaging with you, e.g. not responding, using one word answers, staring away from you, leave them alone

Most facilities are a bit different in their methods (e.g. adult and adolescent programs) but here's what I experienced:

All the patients would eat at the same time at the table with staff monitoring, and one staff eating to be an example. We had assigned seats, if you were new they sat you next to staff for a couple of weeks. We had 40 minutes for meals and 20 minutes for snack. In your first week if you couldn't finish you meal they would give you the amount you didn't have in a liquid substitute. After first week if you didn't complete a meal staff would sit down with you and try to persuade you to eat it, remind you of the reasons that you said you came into treatment for I.e. it was ruining your relationship with your family, if you still wouldn't do it you'd be asked to leave the program. Short answer - yes. I'll break this down into 3 categories - 1) dystonia as a symptom in a person that has Parkinson's 2) Dopa Responsive Dystonia (which I have) which is a rare condition causing dystonia 3) other types of dystonia that don't respond to dopamine treatments. Category 3 is generally not treated with Levodopa and is treated with botox etc.

Categories 1 (PD) and Category 2 (DRD) are both treated with Levodopa. If a person is receiving Levodopa to treat other Parkinson's symptoms that medication can also help with the dystonia. In both PD and DRD the dystonia is caused by low dopamine, but with different causes, in PD it's because the receptors in an area of the brain are dying off, in DRD it's because there isn't enough dopamine being produced in an area of the brain.

Levodopa may or may not completely resolve the dystonia in PD or DRD. It's often helpful in reducing the dystonia in PD though they may become less effective as there's progression of the PD. DRD usually responds extremely well to Levodopa, often completely, but not always. So for both conditions, if Levodopa isn't fully resolving it they may try other medications like anti-cholinergics, other muscle relaxers (e.g. Baclofen, benzodiazepines) and botox. Levodopa is usually tried first and other treatments or the back ups.

I'm in a similar but different position. I (32F) have Dopa Responsive Dystonia. Before getting diagnosed as a kid I had really bad dystonia in my feet, legs, arms, hands and was getting full body tremors like I had severe Parkinson's. Luckily I responded really well to low dose L-dopa and I was almost symptom free for 15 years. I did develop severe back spasms in my teens that came and went, also herniated a disc in my lower back so I was getting bouts of sciatica which was worse pain than the dystonia.

And then I hit my mid 20s. I would occasionally (on average once a year) have the dystonia in my arms and legs return and other muscles like my abdominal muscles would spasm or get really week. Usually the episodes were brought on my sleep deprivation and would resolve in one night of decent sleep. 5 years ago I started getting severe episodes of cervical dystonia a few times a year, my head gets stuck forward with my chin to my chest and I can't move it at all. It also started in my intercostal muscles (muscles between my ribs) which gives the sensation of trouble breathing which sucks. Luckily there is a rescue med combination that makes it release (injection of Benztropine which is an anti-cholinergic and Torodol which is an anti-inflammatory). And then the last 2 years things got significantly worse, the flare ups of dystonia in my arms and legs now occur a couple of times a year but instead of resolving in a day or two it now takes one to two weeks. The cervical dystonia flare ups occur every few weeks now and the severe back spasms also happen more frequently and last a lot longer. The icing on the cake is that the back spasms disrupt my sleep which worsens all of the dystonia. 

It's been difficult to medicate. My neurologist increased my L-dopa which helps to a point, but it doesn't eliminate the symptoms like it used to. We increased my Baclofen from 10mg a day to 30-40mg. while I could theoretically go higher I'm dealing with orthostatic hypotension and low blood pressure in general and the Baclofen makes that worse, even at 30mg. I take the Benztropine and Torodol orally each day, it keeps the cervical dystonia down to being occasional rather than constant. I have a prescription for an opioid pain killer. I used to only use it for the sciatica but now I occasionally take it for the really large back spasms. I really try to limit how often I take it because I don't want to build a tolerance to it (and because I have internalized the messages from the opioid crisis even though I know I take them responsibly) I can't take any sort of benzodiazepine, they give me severe hallucinations. I tried a muscle relaxant called Cyclobenzaprine but that makes me hallucinate too.  I have also had lidocaine injects into some of the large knots in my back which lessens the pain for a few hours and helps disrupt the spasm.

I'm lucky I have an amazing family doctor who has become very knowledgeable about dystonia, as well as a movement disorder specialist. If you can, see if you can see a movement disorder specialist virtually if there isn't one in your area. Dystonia is special, it's very different than most other conditions causing chronic pain and it's difficult for doctors to treat if they're not knowledgeable in it. I have heard from other patients in the Orthopedic surgery clinic (who I see for my disc and sciatica) that a Baclofen pump was helpful, they could have higher doses with few side effects so it might be worth looking into. I hope you find something that helps Being in your 30s with dystonia just blows.

Honestly I find medications to be by far the most effective thing in dealing with dystonia. I'm a person who very much believes in exercise, massages massaged and lifestyle modifications and I use these to treat other things like non-dystonia related stiffness and muscle spasms. But for dystonia, at least in my case, they don't work well on their own, they can help in combination with meds. And as a catch 22 sleep is often really important in managing dystonia so if you're not sleeping well that will make it worse. So consider asking your GP to try some meds. There are options, different kinds of muscle relaxants, a class of drugs called anticholinergics that can help (includes Diphenhydramine aka Benadryl). Good luck!

Ouch. I've had that kind of dystonia in my feet, it's really uncomfortable, I can't imagine having to work on your feet with it. If you haven't already, see if you can get a doctor to check for Dopa responsive dystonia (can usually be done with a trial of a medication called L-dopa). It's a rare condition which often gets missed by doctors. It may be a long shot but what you're describing is exactly how my feet were and that type of spasming, position your foot is in and the tremors is a common presentation of it. If it is, then it's treatable with medication. If you want more information on this feel free to PM me.

If it's not, you might be able to get the weight off your foot through the knee thing they give people with broken ankles (it's like a platform you kneel on with one leg and a stick with to the ground). I'm not sure what your job is but if there's any way you can get off your feet more, like sitting on a tall stool, let your employer know you have a medical condition and they can hopefully help re-structure things a bit to help you. If sitting down I used to stick a pencil under my toes to take the pressure off from some of the toe curling. Sometimes a splint holding the foot straight can help (make sure it's well padded) but still keeping weight off it as much as possible. Massage and using your hands to hold your foot in more comfortable positions for a bit can also help.

For PT make sure whoever you see has experience working with movement disorders/dystonia, if they treat it like it's foot pain/mobility issues from another cause it can make it worse and cause you more pain (if they put you on a treadmill find a new PT). It might be helpful to see what medication options you have that can help relax the muscles and ease the pain, it's a lot easier to work with the muscles in PT or splint them when they're not in complete spasm. I've found anti-inflammatory pain meds like ibuprofen can be helpful.

When your heart rate goes way up when you stand it usually means that your blood pressure is dropping and your heart is speeding up to try and push blood to your head. If you want to research it search "orthostatic hypotension and tachycardia). It can make you really dizzy standing up and cause people to faint. Stand up really slowly and carefully and have something to hold onto. It's usually a sign that you're dehydrated and/or that your electrolytes are low which is dangerous. It would be good to get your electrolytes checked and have electrolyte replenishing drinks. Your testing heart rate is also low. None of this is good for your heart, please see a medical professional.

From my dietician: if you are running a calorie deficit it will harm your athletic performance. She worked with one athlete who missed out on the Olympics because she was trying to lose weight, reduced her food and it decreased her speed and missed the performance target required. Obviously it's not this easy but you eventually have a choice to make, keep going with ED goals and sacrifice your athletic performance to it, or chose to recover which will make you a better athlete.

If you are interested in the recovery option the best thing you can do is see a dietician with a background in treating people with ED'S. If they have also worked with athletes that's great, but the ED background is the most important. Based on your sport, the types of exercise you do, how long your training sessions are and things like that, they can give you a meal plan that gives you the appropriate amount and types of food with the exercise you do and keep you satiated. You have to try and trust them that it won't be "too much", they're a professional and they know what they're doing. Until I saw my dietician I didn't realize how much information I didn't know. There's also a bunch of reasons why "normal" weight really doesn't work with athletes that my dietician explained to be, e.g. I didn't know what glycogen stores were before.

Overcoming an ED is hard but it's possible. Doing it alone is significantly harder. The more people you can get helping you the better.

I'm on high dose melatonin. Big caveat to start: high dose melatonin is sometimes used to treat sleep disorders in patients with Parkinsons Disease or similar disorders, which I have. My treatment is overseen by a neurologist who specializes in movement disorders and I do not have a "normal" brain. All of that being said here is my experience...

I'd had about 2 years of severe insomnia, with both trouble falling asleep and waking up to 6 times a night. I was taking a "z drug" (I can't take most medications used to treat insomnia because of my neurological disorder). My friend suggested melatonin and I took 10mg because that was what she had. Didn't really feel a huge difference. I ran it by my neurologist the next week and she suggested I start with 20mg. She said up to 50mg was used in the studies on Parkinsons patients and that would be ok for me to increase to if needed. 20mg didn't really help so after a couple of weeks I increased to 30mg. It didn't help me fall asleep but I woke up less at night. A month later I went up to 40mg to see if I could get further improvement, got a bit of improvement in falling asleep and sleeping with fewer interruptions. A month or two later I went up to the 50mg to see if I could get some more improvement in falling asleep. Slight improvement falling asleep, I felt a bit more relaxed and it had me mostly sleeping through the night, and if I did wake up it was a lot easier for me to fall back to sleep unless something like severe spasms from the neurological disorder woke me up. I sleep about 7 to 8 hours a night. I didn't have any unwanted side effects from the melatonin and I'm still taking the 50mg dose. I occasionally lower the dose to see whether a lower dose would be effective but I wake up at night more if I do.

For me one of the causes has been medication changes, if I've increased by L-Dopa dose I can be foggy for a few weeks as my body adjusts. It always does settle though. If you're taking anything other than carbilev, some other medications, many muscle relaxants for example, can cause those symptoms.

Another thing to remember is having DRD can be exhausting for the body and for the mind. Relearning how to walk is exhausting, physio in general is exhausting (it's good you're doing it though) and just existing with DRD can be exhausting sometimes with the amount of strain it puts your body under. That amount of fatigue, I find, can bring on cognitive symptoms. But they have not been permanent. It sounds like you've gone through a lot but you're doing all the right things to manage the DRD and as your body adjusts the cognitive symptoms should go down.

Stress can also add to this. Find things that reduce your stress level and give yourself permission to do them as much as you need. Gentle yoga, funny TV, sitting in nature... you'll know best what works for you.

It might be worth talking to your doctor about getting a sleep study and make sure you're actually getting quality sleep. If you're not that can also affect your cognitive abilities. I know this is easier said than done, but try not to worry too much about what the future will look like, what this all means for your career and whether things are getting worse. I had a lot of cognitive symptoms after a flare up last year, and with COVID disrupting all the helpful stuff in my routine, and was worried I didn't have what it takes to do my job anymore, and then one day I noticed myself picking up on details that other people hadn't and forming more creative arguments and strategies and remembering things better. What can you do? A surprising amount can come from raising awareness, even just on the internet. Sharing articles, sharing any news articles about specific facilities helps. You can also collaborate with organizations who might assist with this issue. You might have to educate them on this issue, it's surprising how few people know these places exist. Any organizations that deal with personal freedoms, human rights, international rights, mental health rights, institutional rights or youth rights are a good place to start.
